Model validation

Source: vignettes/model-validation.Rmd
model-validation.Rmd

What does model validation mean?

Validation of an insurance pricing model is broader than comparing fit statistics. A model may describe the estimation data well while producing unstable, weakly supported or actuarially implausible tariff relativities. Conversely, a statistically detectable imperfection may have little practical pricing effect in the insured portfolio.

No single metric determines whether a model is adequate. A validation review normally combines several dimensions:

Dimension Practical question
Statistical adequacy Are the model structure and distribution broadly consistent with the data?
Predictive performance How well does the model predict the relevant outcome, preferably outside the estimation sample where appropriate?
Stability How sensitive are estimates or performance to variation in the observed sample?
Tariff plausibility Are the effects interpretable, credible and suitable for the intended tariff?
Portfolio behaviour Where does expected experience differ systematically from observed experience?

These dimensions are complementary rather than a mandatory sequence. Their relative importance depends on the response, portfolio, modelling objective and intended use of the tariff.

This vignette starts from fitted models. Getting Started provides the worked modelling example, while Pricing workflow and package building blocks maps validation within the wider package. Jump to the quick start for runnable examples.

Validation map

The following functions support different validation questions. Not every model requires every diagnostic.

Validation question Typical tool
How do alternative fitted models compare? model_performance()
Are tariff relativities plausible and sufficiently supported? rating_table()
Does marginal observed experience support the fitted pattern? add_factor_experience()
How sensitive is measured performance to portfolio resampling? validate_performance()
How sensitive are the fitted coefficients to portfolio resampling? coefficient_stability()
Is a Poisson frequency model materially overdispersed? check_overdispersion()
Do simulation-based residuals show remaining structure? check_residuals()
Where does the model over- or under-predict? calibration_analysis()

Compact example setup

Most examples use two Poisson frequency models fitted to the same records, response and exposure definition. Each prediction is an expected claim count for the observed policy period because it includes the earned-exposure offset.

library(insurancerating)

portfolio <- as.data.frame(MTPL2)
portfolio$area <- factor(portfolio$area)
portfolio$area <- set_reference_level(portfolio$area, portfolio$exposure)

intercept_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ 1 + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = portfolio
)

area_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ area + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = portfolio
)

The fitted model is starting material here; construction of frequency, severity and technical risk-premium models is covered elsewhere.

Quick start

Each call answers a different question about the fitted frequency models. The diagnostics can be used independently.

# Compare models fitted on the same records.
fit_comparison <- model_performance(intercept_model, area_model)

# Does one common rate predict the right total in each area?
area_check <- calibration_analysis(intercept_model, portfolio, by = "area")

# How much does prediction error vary on rows left out of each refit?
set.seed(123)
resample_result <- validate_performance(
  area_model, portfolio, sampling = "bootstrap", sample_fraction = 0.8,
  n_resamples = 50, metrics = c("rmse", "mae", "deviance"),
  show_progress = FALSE
)

# Is the response distribution consistent with the fitted model?
residual_check <- check_residuals(area_model, n_simulations = 250)

area_check compares observed and expected counts, with exposure for context. A value of O/E above one means the model predicted too few claims. Here this is a check on the estimation portfolio, not an independent test.

area_check
#>   area Observed   Expected        OE    N   Exposure
#> 1    1      146 143.295924 1.0188706 1194 1065.74795
#> 2    0        1   1.789182 0.5589146   15   13.30685
#> 3    2       98 110.057361 0.8904448  921  818.53973
#> 4    3      113 102.857533 1.0986069  870  764.99178

The resampling plot and residual plot show how to inspect the other results. For sampling variation in individual tariff effects, see coefficient stability.

Comparing model performance 

fit_comparison
#> # Comparison of Model Performance Indices
#> 
#>      Model      |   AIC    |   BIC    | RMSE  | Residual_Deviance 
#> ----------------+----------+----------+-------+------------------ 
#> intercept_model | 2284.056 | 2290.063 | 0.356 |          1608.352 
#>      area_model |  2287.25 | 2311.275 | 0.356 |          1605.545

model_performance() reports AIC, BIC, response-scale RMSE and residual deviance:

  • AIC and BIC compare likelihood fit while penalising model complexity;
  • residual deviance describes the remaining lack of fit on the estimation data;
  • RMSE summarises prediction error in the response unit and gives relatively high weight to large errors because it squares them. The RMSE itself is unweighted. Here the response unit is claim count, not claims per unit exposure.

These values are most directly comparable when models use the same response, estimation records, weights and offsets, as they do here. Residual deviances should also be compared within the same model family. RMSE uses only the rows retained in the fit. None of these values establishes performance on a future portfolio.

Adding area lowers the residual deviance, but both AIC and BIC favour the simpler model once they account for its fewer parameters. The RMSEs are nearly identical. A closer match to historical totals by area is not, by itself, a reason to include area in the tariff. Look at the experience behind the area effects and how well they hold up on other data.

Inspecting tariff structure and observed experience

rating_table() expresses fitted GLM effects as tariff relativities and shows the exposure supporting each level. This makes the statistical output easier to review in actuarial terms. add_factor_experience() adds an observed_relativity column for the table and the corresponding plot.

For this comparison, use MTPL, which also contains policyholder age. The model estimates regional effects at the same age, while the observed frequency reflects each region’s actual mix of ages.

tariff_portfolio <- as.data.frame(MTPL)
tariff_portfolio$zip <- set_reference_level(
  factor(tariff_portfolio$zip), tariff_portfolio$exposure
)

tariff_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ zip + age_policyholder + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(), data = tariff_portfolio
)

tariff_table <- rating_table(
  "Age-adjusted model" = tariff_model,
  model_data = tariff_portfolio,
  exposure = "exposure"
)

tariff_review <- tariff_table |>
  add_factor_experience(
    data = tariff_portfolio,
    risk_factors = "zip",
    claim_count = "nclaims",
    exposure = "exposure",
    metric = "frequency",
    label = "Observed frequency"
  )

tariff_review
#>        risk_factor            level est_Age-adjusted model exposure
#> 1      (Intercept)      (Intercept)              0.3121503       NA
#> 2              zip                0              1.0006508      207
#> 3              zip                1              1.0000000    11081
#> 4              zip                2              0.9020158     7783
#> 5              zip                3              0.9559945     7588
#> 6 age_policyholder age_policyholder              0.9831025       NA
#>   observed_relativity
#> 1                  NA
#> 2           0.9752231
#> 3           1.0000000
#> 4           0.9009127
#> 5           0.9515761
#> 6                  NA
autoplot(
  tariff_review,
  risk_factors = "zip",
  metric = "frequency"
)

A model with slightly better aggregate fit can still be unattractive when it creates volatile neighbouring relativities, extreme effects supported by little exposure or shapes without a plausible risk interpretation. An extreme coefficient in a small segment should therefore not be interpreted in the same way as the same coefficient supported by a substantial share of the portfolio.

For region 0, the observed frequency is about 2.5% below the reference region’s frequency, while the fitted model estimates almost no difference at the same age. Region 0 also has relatively little exposure. The gap is a reason to look at the age mix and claim volume, not evidence by itself of poor calibration. Use calibration_analysis() to compare full-model predictions with actual outcomes.

Assessing resampling stability

Unlike model_performance(), validate_performance() refits the model for each sample. For random resampling, sampling determines how rows are drawn and sample_fraction sets the size of the training draw. A fraction below 1 does not turn a bootstrap into a random split.

sampling sample_fraction Rows used to fit Rows used to score each refit
"bootstrap" (default) 1 (default) Full-size draw with replacement Same bootstrap sample (in sample)
"bootstrap" Below 1 Smaller draw with replacement Rows not used for training (out of bag)
"split" Below 1 Random draw without replacement Remaining rows (held-out test set)
"split" 1 All rows Same rows (no holdout)
"rolling" Not used Earlier periods in an expanding window Subsequent periods

The random methods draw rows, not whole policies. If a policy contributes multiple rows, a held-out row can belong to a policy already seen in training. To assess performance on unseen policies in that setting, form a holdout by policy and keep each policy’s records together.

The quick start uses out-of-bag evaluation. The plot subtitle identifies the evaluation rows used.

head(resample_result$scores)
#>        rmse       mae deviance
#> 1 0.3436239 0.2051759 708.7991
#> 2 0.3715056 0.2115858 746.2368
#> 3 0.3766939 0.2101049 785.8242
#> 4 0.3584633 0.2047888 761.8024
#> 5 0.3542650 0.2069595 716.3567
#> 6 0.3422794 0.2106021 687.1987
autoplot(resample_result, metric = "rmse")

With sampling = "bootstrap", sample_fraction = 0.8, the initial draw is 80 rows per 100, with replacement. Some rows can be drawn more than once, so the out-of-bag set is not a fixed 20% of the data. With sampling = "split", sample_fraction = 0.8, the initial draw selects 80 distinct rows per 100 and holds out the rest. For either design, rows added to the training sample to cover missing factor levels are excluded from held-out scoring.

RMSE and MAE measure error in claim counts here. The dashed orange line is the original model’s RMSE on the full supplied portfolio, not on the out-of-bag rows used for the histogram. The table also reports predictive deviance: the same calculation as residual deviance, applied to the evaluation rows and their predictions. Total deviance depends on the number and weight of those rows as well as prediction quality.

A wide spread of scores may reflect differences between refitted models, differences in the claim mix of the evaluation samples, or both. Use coefficient_stability() to examine the fitted effects themselves. Evaluation on out-of-bag or split rows is out of sample for each refit, but does not replace validation on a later or external portfolio.

How stable are the tariff relativities?

coefficient_stability() draws rows with replacement from the estimation portfolio and refits the GLM. It summarises the fitted effects, not prediction errors. For this log-link model, scale = "relativity" expresses each area effect as a ratio to the original reference area.

area_stability <- coefficient_stability(
  area_model, n_resamples = 100, seed = 123, show_progress = FALSE
)
autoplot(area_stability, scale = "relativity")

The dots are original GLM estimates, the bars are bootstrap intervals, and the dashed line at 1 marks no relative effect. The counts next to each term show how many of the requested resamples yield comparable estimates for that effect. Use summary(area_stability, scale = "relativity") to inspect the numbers. A refit can converge without yielding a comparable estimate for every level, for example when a reference level is absent from the draw. A narrow interval based on few usable draws offers little reassurance. Area 0 has about 13 policy-years and one claim in the estimation portfolio, so interpret its interval with that limited experience in mind.

This is a row bootstrap, not a policy bootstrap. If one policy contributes several records, drawing them independently can understate uncertainty. When that dependence matters, a cluster bootstrap would draw whole policies and retain their records together. coefficient_stability() does not currently implement that design.

Testing on later periods

Use the same simulated portfolio to answer two different questions: did a model kept fixed after 2022 continue to predict the right number of claims, and how well would the same specification predict the next year if refitted each year? In this example the underlying claim frequency rises in 2023.

set.seed(123)
temporal_data <- data.frame(
  year = rep(2020:2025, each = 250),
  exposure = rep(c(0.5, 1), 750)
)
temporal_data$nclaims <- with(
  temporal_data,
  rpois(nrow(temporal_data), exposure * ifelse(year < 2023, 0.10, 0.20))
)
historical_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ 1 + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(), data = subset(temporal_data, year <= 2022)
)

Calibration of a fixed model

Fit once on 2020 to 2022 and use that fit unchanged to predict later years. calibration_analysis() compares the resulting claim totals with the observed totals in each year.

year_calibration <- calibration_analysis(
  historical_model, subset(temporal_data, year > 2022), by = "year"
)
year_calibration
#>   year Observed Expected       OE   N Exposure
#> 1 2023       28 18.33333 1.527273 250    187.5
#> 2 2024       31 18.33333 1.690909 250    187.5
#> 3 2025       34 18.33333 1.854545 250    187.5
autoplot(year_calibration)

In 2023, the historical model expects about 18 claims and 28 are observed (O/E 1.53). The fixed rate underpredicts that year’s claims. The plot checks the prediction level, not how well the model ranks individual risks.

Performance of rolling refits

Rolling validation refits the same formula as more years become available. It uses the original fit as a model specification, not as the source of the predictions.

validate_performance(
  historical_model, temporal_data, sampling = "rolling", time = "year",
  initial = 3, metrics = c("rmse", "mae", "deviance"), show_progress = FALSE
)
#>   iteration train_start train_end test_start test_end n_train n_test      rmse
#> 1         1        2020      2022       2023     2023     750    250 0.3297975
#> 2         2        2020      2023       2024     2024    1000    250 0.3843832
#> 3         3        2020      2024       2025     2025    1250    250 0.3968839
#>         mae deviance
#> 1 0.1689067 130.2780
#> 2 0.1866373 139.2036
#> 3 0.2028800 148.2633

The first fit uses 2020 to 2022 and scores 2023. The next fit adds 2023 to training and scores 2024. Each score uses a different test year. A change in RMSE across years can reflect a change in claim experience as well as a change in the fit. To compare alternative specifications, test them on the same windows.

Checking distributional assumptions

Overdispersion 

dispersion_check <- check_overdispersion(area_model)
dispersion_check
#> Dispersion ratio =    1.220
#> Pearson's Chi-squared = 3655.711
#> p-value =  < 0.001
#> Overdispersion detected.

For a Poisson frequency GLM, the dispersion ratio is Pearson’s chi-squared statistic divided by the residual degrees of freedom. A value above one means that observed variation exceeds the variance implied by the Poisson model. Here the ratio is about 1.22. It is a diagnostic of extra variation, not a factor to apply to premiums.

Both statistical evidence and practical magnitude matter. In a large insurance portfolio, a small departure can produce a very small p-value simply because many observations are available. The size of the dispersion ratio and its effect on uncertainty and tariff decisions are generally more informative than the p-value alone. Overdispersion can indicate omitted heterogeneity, clustering, unusual observations or model misspecification, but does not by itself identify the cause.

Simulation-based residuals 

autoplot(residual_check)
#> Residuals consistent with expected distribution (p = 0.656)

check_residuals() uses DHARMa simulations from the fitted model to construct scaled residuals. The QQ plot and uniformity test assess whether the observed response behaves consistently with the distribution implied by that model.

The QQ plot can flag a distributional mismatch but does not identify the predictor or segment involved. A separate plot against fitted values, exposure or a rating factor can help locate a pattern. The uniformity p-value is a diagnostic signal, not a stand-alone acceptance rule.

Reviewing observed versus expected experience

Use calibration_analysis() to compare observed and expected outcomes overall and within segments. Here the predictions include earned exposure, so both totals are claim counts.

calibration_analysis(intercept_model, portfolio)
#>   Observed Expected OE    N Exposure
#> 1      358      358  1 3000 2662.586
autoplot(area_check)

O/E is observed claims divided by expected claims. A ratio above 1 means more claims were observed than expected; a ratio below 1 means fewer. The overall ratio describes calibration-in-the-large.

The model with one common frequency matches the overall claim total on its estimation data, but it does not match every area. In area 3 it expects about 103 claims, compared with 113 observed. Area 0 is farther from O/E = 1, but has only one observed claim and about 13 policy-years. A larger gap is not necessarily a stronger signal.

If you instead evaluate area_model on its estimation data, O/E is 1 in every area because the model fits a separate rate for each. That is not evidence of calibration on new data.

For a single calendar-year grouping, see Calibration of a fixed model. To check whether the pattern differs by area, use by = c("year", "area"). This gives one row per observed year and area combination, with their exposure and claim totals. The plot shows a point per combination rather than joining areas into a single time series.

Does the model get claim frequency right at different risk levels?

For this example, reserve part of the MTPL portfolio and fit a frequency model using age and ZIP on the remaining rows. The row split illustrates evaluation on data not used in the fit; it is not a test on a later year.

With groups = 5, the function sorts policy records from lowest to highest predicted claims per policy-year. Dividing each prediction by its exposure for this ranking means a longer policy period is not treated as a higher risk just because more claims are expected during it.

The sorted records are split into five groups. Group 1 contains the lowest predicted risks and group 5 the highest. Each group aims for about 20% of the portfolio’s total exposure, not 20% of the policies. These are groups of model predictions, not rating-factor levels such as area. Policies with the same predicted frequency can fall on either side of a group boundary; ties follow the input row order.

set.seed(123)
train <- sample.int(nrow(tariff_portfolio), floor(0.7 * nrow(tariff_portfolio)))
risk_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ age_policyholder + zip + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(), data = tariff_portfolio[train, ]
)
risk_calibration <- calibration_analysis(
  risk_model, tariff_portfolio[-train, ], groups = 5
)
knitr::kable(risk_calibration, digits = 2)
Group Observed Expected OE N Exposure
1 154 147.18 1.05 1728 1597.47
2 190 186.30 1.02 1767 1597.88
3 192 218.70 0.88 1801 1597.85
4 227 253.48 0.90 1854 1598.29
5 314 301.17 1.04 1850 1597.70 
autoplot(risk_calibration)

Each dot is one group. Its x-coordinate is total expected claims divided by the group’s total policy-years; its y-coordinate is total observed claims divided by the same policy-years. Group 3 (the middle dot) has 192 observed claims versus about 219 expected. A dot below the diagonal means the model predicted too many claims for that group; a dot above it means the model predicted too few.

This is a visual check for systematic over- or under-prediction, not a statistical test or a measure of how well the model ranks individual risks. Read a gap alongside the group’s exposure and claim volume: a large O/E deviation based on few claims may have little credibility. If multiple rows describe the same policy, keep them together when forming a holdout.

Validation, investigation and refinement

Comparing expected claims before and after refinement

For a model returned by refit(), the original portfolio may not contain the columns added by smoothing or restrictions. To check the refit’s own portfolio, use extract_model_data(refined_model). For a smoothed model, group by the column containing the new tariff bands (for example, by = "age_smooth" if the source variable was age), rather than by the numeric relativity column used in the offset. On separate evaluation data, apply the same refinement mappings to those rows first.

To check a restriction, put observed claims, expected claims before and expected claims after side by side. Use the same records and the same grouping column for both models so that any change comes from the predictions rather than a change in portfolio mix.

restricted_model <- prepare_refinement(area_model, data = portfolio) |>
  add_restriction(c("3" = 1.10), model_variable = "area") |>
  refit()

evaluation <- extract_model_data(restricted_model)
before <- calibration_analysis(area_model, evaluation, by = "area")
after <- calibration_analysis(restricted_model, evaluation, by = "area")

comparison <- merge(
  before[c("area", "Exposure", "Observed", "Expected")],
  after[c("area", "Expected")],
  by = "area",
  suffixes = c("_before", "_after")
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 2)
area Exposure Observed Expected_before Expected_after
0 13.31 1 1 0.99
1 1065.75 146 146 145.08
2 818.54 98 98 97.38
3 764.99 113 113 114.55

Use fixed bands or rating-factor levels for this comparison. With groups = 5, each model can rank policies differently, so its group 1 need not contain the same policies as group 1 from the other model. This is a comparison of two sets of predictions on the same portfolio, not evidence that the restriction improves predictions on new data.

Acting on validation findings

A diagnostic can identify the observations or tariff levels worth a closer look. The follow-up depends on the cause: incorrect exposure may call for a data correction, while missing interactions or an unsuitable distribution may call for a different model. Neither necessarily calls for a tariff refinement. If there is a separate actuarial reason to change a fitted effect, the Refinement building blocks vignette shows how to record, refit and review that adjustment. The same diagnostics can be reused after a change to the data, model or tariff.

Putting the evidence together

Validation should combine evidence rather than rank models on one metric. A model may have a slightly lower AIC but unstable coefficients, weak observed support and material residual structure. Such a model may be less suitable for tariff implementation than a more stable alternative.

Conversely, a statistically significant diagnostic result may have little practical effect when its magnitude is small and portfolio behaviour remains stable. The conclusion should reflect statistical adequacy, predictive evidence, sampling stability, exposure and credibility, actuarial plausibility and the intended pricing use.
